conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Today I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it helps us understand what support might be most helpful to you right now.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. If at any point a question feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll go at your pace.

Shall we begin?  
Thinking back over the past week, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*shifts in chair, eyes a bit tired but trying to smile*

Um... honestly? Not very often. I mean, I *want* to laugh—my husband still makes his same dumb jokes—but it just feels kind of... flat? Like the baby will do something silly and everyone else chuckles, but I’m just too exhausted to really feel it. Maybe once or twice this week I actually laughed out loud. Mostly I just feel like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small, tired shrug*

Yeah… not really. I mean, I *tried*—my sister sent one of those ridiculous cat videos yesterday—but it barely got a smile out of me. I just felt… too worn-out to care.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*quiet for a beat, then speaks softly*

Not much… I keep telling myself I *should* be excited about little things—like the baby’s bath time or the walk we planned to the park—but when it actually comes, it just feels like another chore. I used to look forward to my morning coffee, and now I drink it because I need the caffeine, not because I enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes fixed on my hands*

Yeah... a few times. Like yesterday, when she wouldn't settle for her nap and I ended up rocking her for an hour. My husband found us both crying and he took her, but all I could think was, "Other moms figure this out—why can't I?" I know it's probably not fair to blame myself, but the thought just pops in: *I must be doing something wrong.*
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods, rubbing my palms together*

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s this low buzz in my chest that won’t quit. Half the time I couldn’t even tell you what I’m anxious about—just a constant fear that something’s wrong with the baby or that I’ll miss some cue and she’ll get sick. Last night I kept checking if she was breathing every twenty minutes, even though she’s perfectly fine. I *know* it’s irrational, but I can’t shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifts uncomfortably*

A couple of times… like the other afternoon when she wouldn’t stop crying and my heart just started racing. It came out of nowhere—no real danger, just this sudden wave of *panic* that I wouldn’t be able to soothe her. I had to hand her to my mom and go sit on the porch until my chest stopped feeling so tight.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly, voice a little shaky*

Yeah… most days, honestly. It’s not that anything huge is wrong—just the constant feeding, changing, trying to get her to sleep, worrying if she’s gaining enough weight… it all piles up. By dinner time I feel like I’m drowning in tiny, never-ending tasks. Some mornings I open my eyes and the first thing I feel is dread about getting through the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes looking a little glazed*

Several nights this week. I’ll finally get her down and crawl into bed, but then my mind just… races. I keep replaying every little thing—did I burp her long enough, is she too hot, too cold, when will she wake up again—and before I know it an hour’s passed. I probably fall asleep around two, then I’m up again at four when she stirs. It’s not that I’m wide-awake happy or sad, more like I can’t shut the worry off long enough to drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable

*swallows hard, eyes misting*

Yeah… I have. It hits most in the evenings, after the visitors stop texting and it’s just me and the baby. I’ll look at her little face and instead of this rush of love I keep expecting, I just feel… empty. I keep thinking, *I should be grateful—she’s healthy, I’m okay—so why do I feel so down?* I cried in the shower yesterday for no real reason; the sadness just sits on my chest like a weight.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*voice drops to almost a whisper*

Once… night before last. She wouldn’t latch, and I kept trying and trying until we were both sobbing. I finally just put her in the bassinet, safe, and went to the bathroom so my husband wouldn’t hear me fall apart. I cried until my throat hurt. It felt like all the tiredness and worry just spilled out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—never. I get overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again… to be able to enjoy my baby instead of feeling so heavy all the time.

I hear how hard these early weeks have been: the constant worry, the hollow sadness that arrives each evening, the feeling that even simple joys are out of reach. You are working so hard to care for your daughter while battling an invisible weight on your chest, and you still took the time to share your experience today-an act of courage that shows your deep love for her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to enjoy humor despite effort, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-total loss of anticipatory enjoyment, describing even previously pleasant activities as chores and noting absence of excitement, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated self-blaming "a few times" with a concrete example and persistent intrusive thoughts of inadequacy, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-constant, irrational worry and physical tension, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden, unexplained panic that led to physical symptoms and needing to hand off the baby, matching "Yes, sometimes" (score 2).</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most days, unable to cope with routine tasks, and experiencing dread—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating sleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness, evening lows, emotional emptiness, and unexplained crying, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 22 places you well above the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major depression. You endorse core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest (<quote>it just feels like another chore</quote>), daily sadness (<quote>sadness just sits on my chest like a weight</quote>), guilt (<quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>), and multiple somatic/functional impacts (sleep, crying, panic, overwhelm). Combined with prominent anxiety and panic, this presentation exceeds moderate risk and warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> this week to discuss medication and therapy options
2. Ask about expedited referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist familiar with breastfeeding-compatible treatments
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>; many programs offer virtual sessions during nap times
4. Plan daily 15-minute support blocks-accept help with chores or night feeds so you can rest; sleep deprivation intensifies both depression and anxiety
5. Practice brief grounding skills when panic rises: slow breathing to a 4-6 count, naming five things you can see/hear/feel; share this plan with your partner
6. Limit information overload: choose one trusted parenting source, set a social-media curfew, and focus on 'good-enough' rather than perfect baby care
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after starting treatment; improvement often begins within days of the right intervention
8. Keep national support numbers handy: Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773) and 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for 24/7 confidential support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire (10 items)  

### Areas endorsed above threshold  
- **Anhedonia**: minimal amusement, no anticipatory enjoyment  
- **Low mood**: daily sadness, evening “emptiness,” frequent crying  
- **Subjective guilt / inadequacy**: self-blame when baby fussy (“other moms figure this out”)  
- **Persistent anxiety**: near-constant “buzz,” excessive checking, checking breathing q20 min  
- **Panic symptoms**: sudden racing heart, chest tightness when baby cries  
- **Overwhelm / poor coping**: daily tasks feel “drowning,” morning dread  
- **Sleep disturbance**: initial insomnia after night feeds, 2 h latency, racing thoughts  
- **Crying spells**: twice in past week, one episode “until throat hurt”  

### Safety screen  
- Denies self-harm thoughts (Q10).  
- No current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan.  

### Pattern summary  
Presentation consistent with probable **major depressive episode with peripartum onset**, complicated by prominent anxiety and mild panic symptoms. Functional impairment evident in sleep, self-care, and infant-care confidence.  

### Risk factors noted  
- Primiparity, infant feeding difficulties, social comparison, minimal enjoyment in motherhood role.  
- Moderate-to-severe symptom intensity by self-report; warrants expedited mental-health evaluation and support intervention.
